They seem to come from only a few remote parts of our galaxy . <p> Now researchers believe they have tracked down their source : a small , dense star called a white dwarf that is pulling material from its larger and less dense companion star . The material spirals in and produces the blasts , researchers believe . <p> " For the first time we have pinpointed the origin of these signals , confirming the source to be a ' cataclysmic variable ' , or an accreting white dwarf star , " said said Kovi Rose , a PhD student at the University of Sydney who led the discovery .. <p> " Long-period radio transients have puzzled astronomers for years . We 've only found about a dozen , and their origins have been unclear . Now , we 've been able to show that the source for one of these transients @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ companion star . " <p> The system found in the study , named ASKAP J1745-5051 , is made up of the two stars , orbiting each other extremely closely . As they interact , the material from the latter star is heated up and sends out X-rays , and the two stars ' magnetic fields produce the regular radio bursts . <p> Previously , researchers have thought the blasts would be coming from slow-spinning neutron stars known as pulsars . But newer work has suggested that stars rotating so slowly should not be able to produce such signals . <p> Scientists hope that the work will also prove to be a useful way of understanding other such signals , by helping to decode them . <p> The work is reported in a new paper , ' Periodic radio and X-ray emission from an accreting white dwarf binary ' , published in the journal Nature Astronomy .

@@137718660 <h> As he captures the sounds of British birds for a new book , BAFTA-winning sound recordist Chris Watson recalls his travels with the TV legend <p> Not many people can say they have stood on the North Pole with Sir David Attenborough , collaborated with Yoko Ono and won Baftas for their ground-breaking work on nature shows . But that 's all been part and parcel of a hugely varied life for sound recordist Chris Watson . Chris , 72 , has worked with Sir David capturing wildlife sounds on everything from The Life of Birds to Frozen Planet , Kingdom and The Green Planet . <p> Now he has turned his attention closer to home , to birds on our doorstep that are either in decline or endangered . @@137719948 <p> The concepts of green buildings and sustainable cities emerged globally during the 1970s environmental movement , sparked by the 1973 oil crisis and a growing awareness of resource depletion and ecological damage . <p> These terminologies were formally introduced to bridge the gap between rapid urban development and environmental preservation , providing a standardised framework to combat climate change , reduce massive energy consumption , and curb carbon emissions . <p> While ' green building ' focuses on the micro-level utilising eco-friendly materials , water conservation , and energy efficiency within individual structures ' sustainable cities ' scales these ideas to the macro-level , integrating green infrastructure , public transit , and waste management into a cohesive urban ecosystem . <p> Green buildings and sustainable cities are deeply connected in Oman 's urban planning , acting as the fundamental building blocks for the nation 's eco-friendly future . As urban population grows , the Sultanate faces rising energy demands , water scarcity , and high temperatures . To address these challenges , Oman is integrating green building practices into its broader urban strategies to create resilient , low-carbon cities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for sustainable development . A major pillar of this vision is the creation of sustainable , smart cities that protect natural resources and mitigate the impacts of climate change . Individual green buildings are the structural units that make this vision possible . A city can not achieve true sustainability if its individual structures consume excessive energy and water . By adopting green building standards , Oman ensures that new urban developments actively contribute to national environmental targets . <p> Water scarcity is another critical challenge in the region . Green buildings feature advanced water-saving fixtures and greywater recycling systems . The treated wastewater is reused for landscaping and cooling towers across the community . @@137775347 <h> ABBA ( All Boys Believe Anything ) -- Andy Miller On Voyage <p> I have measured out my life with coffee spoons ; I know the voices dying with a dying fallBeneath the music from a farther room . So how should I presume ? <p> T.S . Eliot -- ' The Love Song Of J. Alfred Prufrock ' <p> On Friday , November 5 , 2021 , while the eyes of the world were on COP26 , its ears were otherwise engaged . And although rare examples may continue to survive in protected environments such as The Quietus , we are unlikely ever again to see herds of opinion of the sort that were once so commonplace sweeping dyspeptically across the pages of NME , Melody Maker , Record Mirror , Sounds and many more . ABBA has outlived them all . <p> In this piece , I had intended to write about what ABBA have meant to me over the last 50 years while also trying to trace what ABBA have meant to the culture during the same period . But the more I thought about it , the more I realised it was impossible for me @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ divorce myself from the culture . There were always three of us in this marriage . <p> The release of Voyage , then , the first new ABBA album since The Visitors in 1981 , prompts three questions , the answers to which may surprise you : <p> Have ABBA made a good album ? Irrelevant . <p> Have ABBA made a good ABBA album ? Debatable . <p> Have ABBA made an ABBA album ? Yes they have . <p> Now that that 's settled , we will unpack those answers and put them together like IKEA furniture , IKEA being another globe-straddling , Kroner-generating Swedish brand , the name of which derives from the identity and goals of its founders i.e. Ingvar Kamprad Emulates ABBA . This is a stupid lie , of course , but it may yet reveal a profound truth . <p> 1 . Have ABBA made a good album ? <p> In the 1970s , few people thought of ABBA as an albums act , a situation that so frustrated Benny and Bj ? rn that they even resorted to naming ABBA 's fifth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ good because of all the hit singles on it . The only listeners who really looked forward to ABBA 's album were children with a Christmas list on the go , which is why to this day all ABBA albums are released in November . <p> No , ABBA were a hit single machine . This may have endeared them to record buyers but those listeners who received their records for free mostly hated the group . Reviewing Greatest Hits in Village Voice in 1976 , Robert Christgau could write , " The band 's real tradition is the advertising jingle , and I 'm sure their disinclination to sing like Negroes endears them to the Europopuli " ; on the release of Greatest Hits Vol. 2 three years later , he was unambiguously hostile : " We have met the enemy and they are them . " And while ABBA did have pockets of support within the rock establishment -- e.g. the ' Dancing Queen ' piano flourishes of Elvis Costello 's ' Oliver 's Army ' or Pete Townshend 's somewhat cagey endorsement of ' SOS ' ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that it was ABBA . But it was too late , because I was already transported by it . " ) -- the prejudice remained . ABBA were inauthentic , naff and ineluctably Swedish ; a cheap and cheerful flat pack forgery . ABBA were not a real group . <p> Towards the end of the decade , as ABBA matured in sound and its members divorced , more critical respect was shown towards the craft and the sadness of records like ' The Winner Takes It All ' , though often it proved hard to write about them without sniggering over Agnetha 's enunciation of the word " apologise " rather than focus on her virtuoso , emotionally-charged performance . Meanwhile on BBC 2 's Not The Nine O'Clock News , a popular satire programme mostly written by and starring the Oxbridge graduates who could n't get into NME , the group was lampooned in the song ' Supa Dupa ' , opening couplet : ' One of us is ugly , one of us is cute / One of us you 'd like to see in her birthday @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wish to be complicit in the abuse retrospectively . I wonder if the subject ever came up . ) <p> The Visitors is now widely judged to be ABBA 's best album , a dimly-lit , chilly collection of songs reflecting political upheaval in Eastern Europe , the emotional estrangement of Frida and Benny and Bj ? rn and Agnetha , and the imminent demise of the group . And the music is glacial , the apex of ABBA 's late analogue synth sound . Yet when the LP was released in late 1981 , I can well recall people having a good old snark about it . Here they come again with one of their November albums , looking all middle-aged and singing about their divorces over a Bontempi organ backing track . Ugh , there 's one about being " not too old for sex " ( ' When All Is Said And Done ' ) . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , spew " ( ' Slipping Through My Fingers ' ) . " THERE IS A WEIRD SONG ABOUT ONE OF THE MEN DATING A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER WITH A STUPID LITTLE COMEDY CIRCUS BIT AT THE END AHAHAHAHA " ( ' Two For The Price Of One ' ) . " Now please excuse me , I must listen to the innovative new sounds of The Human League 's Dare , which I read about in Smash Hits and which was released in October , a much more futuristic month than November . <p> The game was nearly up . Two further singles relatively few people liked or understood were released in 1982 , ' The Day Before You Came ' and ' Under Attack ' , and then the group went on hiatus for 40 years . Critical judgement had been handed down . ABBA were pop music in translation and always would be . <p> But this verdict would be overturned on appeal . <p> 2 . Have ABBA made a good ABBA album ? <p> For most of the 1980s , no one gave a fuck @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ circa 1985 , noticing that several of the group 's early albums had been issued on CD , still the exciting new format then , and thinking this was absurd . Who would want to listen to these relics of ' the decade that taste forgot ' ever again , let alone in perfect sound ( sic ) ? ? I purchased Let Them Eat Bog Shed and moved on . <p> The story of ABBA 's rehabilitation -- or perhaps just its habilitation -- over the following decade is by now familiar . The beats are as follows . The Australian tribute group Bj ? rn Again wind up supporting Nirvana at the Reading Festival ; Erasure 's Abba-esque EP charts in 1992 ; Knowing Me Knowing You with Alan Partridge airs first on radio , then on TV ; Benny and Bj ? rn join U2 on stage in Stockholm for a version of ' Dancing Queen ' ; ABBA Gold is released to runaway sales , followed a year later by More ABBA Gold ; P.J. Hogan 's film Muriel 's Wedding is released in 1994 ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the huge success of Mamma Mia ! on stage in the West End where , 22 years later , it is still running to packed houses . The publication in 2001 of Bright Lights , Dark Shadows , Carl Magnus Palm 's definitive biography of the group , seemed to complete the process . <p> Robert Christgau 's response to all this was simply to pretend that none of it was happening and pray that people would soon come to their senses and start listening to A+ music from Iris DeMent and Moby . In the UK , meanwhile , the generation of music writers who had grown up with ABBA was now coming of age . Alongside essays on Todd Rundgren ( A Wizard , A True Star ) , The Go-Betweens ( Liberty Belle &amp; The Black Diamond Express ) and The Raincoats ( their self-titled debut ) , it included @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ favourably to Sister Lovers , In Utero and The Holy Bible : " The Visitors goes beyond sinister . In 1999 ! <p> In other words , the answer to the question of whether , with Voyage , ABBA have made a good ABBA album wo n't be found in the archives of the music press or its readers ' notions of what constituted ' real music ' . It 's almost @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is neither whether Voyage is a good album nor whether Voyage is a good ABBA album -- at the time of writing , it is outselling the rest of the UK Top 40 combined , reports NME -- but what does it signify that , after a break of 40 years , these four musicians have reconvened in their seventies ? What does it mean for them and for their audience ? <p> 3 . Have ABBA made an ABBA album ? <p> The great Canadian writer Miriam Toews 's new novel Fight Night includes the following scene that may help us arrive at a satisfactory conclusion . Our narrator is an anxious nine-year-old girl called Swiv who has accompanied her grandmother to the beauty salon for a manicure , pedicure and haircut . <p> Then Grandma had her electrolysis and it was terrible to see . I could n't watch . Roxanne had a sharp needle she plugged in and then zapped Grandma 's chin and upper lip with it . I asked Grandma if it hurt and she said hardly ! Everything made her laugh . Even if @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and down . Roxanne had to take a break from zapping for Grandma 's head to stop . Roxanne was very patient . She put on music by a band called ABBA while we waited for Grandma . Grandma said she knew that band ! I thought she was lying to make Roxanne feel good but then she started singing along to a song called ' Chiquitita ' . She sang in a serious , dramatic way , the way she helps Mom rehearse her lines . The first line of the song was about this girl being tied up with her own sorrow . Grandma sang all the verses , she was getting more and more dramatic with every verse . Then Roxanne started singing with her . She knew the words , too ! They both looked at me while they sang like they were trying to tell me something urgent . <p> I do n't even like ' Chiquitita ' , but there it is again , saving someone 's world . <p> As several commentators have pointed out , if you grew up in the 1970s @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and so hearing ' I Still Have Faith In You ' for the first time a few weeks ago was a particularly moving experience . Dave Grohl says he cried and so did I. More than the song , it was the sound that did it , that unique combination of voices , harmony , melody and melancholy . The years did not fall away as you listened ; instead they effortlessly glided into the music itself . It sounded exactly like ABBA because ... it really was ABBA , slightly worn , dignified , and not too old for sex . <p> Ageing alongside the musicians whose work you have been hearing since childhood is , unsurprisingly , an experience that grows deeper as both you and they get older . For the generation born in the late ' 60s and early ' 70s , it is probably ABBA and Kate Bush who encapsulate this . As a ' 70s kid , you did n't have to like their records , though many of us did . Their presence was inescapable , all over radio and TV , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and in the playground . So we do associate them with our childhood(s) . But they have also become the way we 've measured out our lives . When , in 2011 , Kate Bush released 50 Words For Snow , my first thought on hearing it was not , ' Oh , this is a step on from Aerial ' , or ' Hmm , I 'm not sure this hits the heights of Hounds Of Love ' , it was : ' This is the same woman who made The Kick Inside , which I borrowed from the library , who was always on the TV in our living room ; we 're both still here ' . It was the same feeling , vertiginous and emotional , I had while watching her sit at the piano and sing ' Among Angels ' at the close of the Before The Dawn show at Hammersmith in 2014 . This is the same person . <p> Listening to Voyage amplifies and multiplies that feeling of recognition , uncannily . These are the same people in the same group I listened @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ school . But listening to Voyage also reminds us of something we may have forgotten about ABBA . There was always something awkward about them , in their syntax , their subject matter , their presentation , their translation of rock &amp; roll , Phil Spector , disco , Schlager and operetta into their own pop idiom . On side two of Voyage there is a rather mawkish ballad called ' Bumblebee ' , sung beautifully by Frida ; it ought not to fly but it does . Which is also the essence of ABBA itself . <p> The lights are on , it 's time to go . Take another look at that paragraph from Miriam Toews 's Fight Night above and you 'll see the whole story there . Firstly ABBA 's music speaks directly to generations of women , be they children , mother or grandmothers . ( This was demonstrated twenty years ago by the phenomenal success of the stage version of Mamma Mia ! , which was produced by Judy Craymer , written by Catherine Johnson and directed by Phyllida Lloyd , the same team @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ welcome , of course , but not really necessary . And secondly , not only have ABBA made an ABBA album , they have produced the only album ABBA could produce at this point and keep faith with themselves . Because Voyage is an album by , for and about grandparents . Songs like ' Little Things ' and ' Do n't Shut Me Down ' address the subject explicitly ; in this context , the different musical styles feel as though they have been retrieved from somewhere or like snapshots in a photo album . Is this deeply sentimental ? Yes . Is it the stuff of pop music ? Well , it has n't been before but thanks to ABBA , now it is . <p> The new ABBA album is the sound of two songwriters and two singers gracefully , not to say gratefully , approaching old age and facing that " music from a farther room " together with their audience . I would like to think the sun on the cover is rising rather than setting .

@@137845493 <h> Four unbelievable airports from around the world <p> Airports are gateways to far-off lands . Full of hustle and bustle as people rush to make flights or meet family and friends in arrivals . <p> Many of these transport hubs can look and feel very similar . But some airports offer truly dramatic and exciting backdrops for your take-off or landing . <p> BBC Bitesize turns off the auto-pilot in search of some of the most awesome and extreme airports out there . <p> Image caption , <p> The first planes landed on the sand in the wide bay of Traigh Mhor in June 1936 <h> Barra , Scotland <p> Getting to the beach by lunchtime is the dream for many holiday makers - but what if you could literally land on the beach ? On the idyllic Scottish island of Barra , that 's exactly what happens ! <p> White sand , stunning landscapes and crystal-clear waters - this island has it all . Visitors come from all over to take in the breath-taking scenery , literally doing so when they first step off the plane . Because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ island 's beautiful beaches doubles up as the airport , runaway and all . <p> Barra is widely recognised as the only airport in the world that uses a tidal beach as the location for commercial planes to land . That 's right , no tarmac , just sand . <p> This tiny airport was officially opened in 1974 . It 's located on Traigh Mhor ( translating from Gaelic as ' big beach ' ) close to Eoligarry in the north of the island . There are three short runways in the sand , marked with wooden poles at their ends . Though when the Atlantic Ocean tide comes in and submerges the sand it 's hard to imagine an aircraft landing here at all . <p> With only two flights arriving a day ( all scheduled at the mercy of tidal patterns and weather conditions ) Barra airport is n't the busiest , making the beach a great place to take some sea-air . Thankfully a trusty windsock signals to the public when it 's safe to be on the sand and when you need to stay clear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Airport served 167,533 passengers <h> Longyearbyen , Svalbard <p> Thought the first airport on this list was cool ? Well , this next one is much cooler . <p> The Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is located high up in the arctic sea . It 's home to glaciers , the Northern Lights , the midnight sun and winter temperatures of close to -30C . <p> It 's also where you 'll find the world 's most northerly permanent settlement , the town of Longyearbyen . People visit here in their thousands every year hoping for a glimpse of the aurora borealis and much more . And where there 's visitors , there 's an airport . Like the town , it is said to be the world 's northernmost with scheduled flights . <p> The runway here is built on a layer of permafrost ( ground that is permanently frozen ) . However , in 2025 the airport 's operators suggested that the runway could be at risk as a result of the effects of climate change . <p> The pilots and crew often have to contend with snow blizzards @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the passengers , once they 've disembarked , their attention should quickly turn to the warning signs about the polar bears that roam Svalbard . Especially if they somehow miss the fake one at the baggage carousel ! <h> Juanacho E. Yrasquin Airport , Saba <p> Next we 're jetting south-west from Svalbard on a flight from the northernmost commercial runway , to what is believed to be the world 's shortest . ( Note , no flights actually operate between the two ! ) <p> Saba is a tiny volcanic island located in the Caribbean Sea . The island offers amazing diving and hiking opportunities for visitors . Once they manage to get there that is ! <p> Although it 's possible to arrive by ferry , those looking for an extra thrill might consider jetting in on a locally operated propeller plane . To land here , pilots need to negotiate landing on a strip of tarmac that is just 1,312 feet ( roughly 400 metres . ) For context , the smaller of Heathrow Airport 's two runways is just over 12,000 feet ! <p> Some pilots @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trying to land a bird on a postage stamp " . The runway is not only short but also has sheer sea-cliff drops on three sides ! Yeah , you 'll find us on the boat . <h> Tenzing-Hillary Airport , Nepal <p> High up in the Himalayas of Nepal is the small town of Lukla . Many adventurers give this place the nickname ' the gateway to Everest ' and it 's here that one the world 's most dangerous airports can be found . <p> Lukla airport , or Tenzing-Hillary airport , as it has been known since being renamed in 2008 , sits at an elevation of nearly 3,000 metres above sea-level . Its more modern name pays homage to explorers Tenzing Norgay and Sir Edmund Hillary , the first confirmed people to ever reach the summit of Everest . <p> Lukla 's runway is just 527 metres long by 20 metres wide . At one end there 's a mountain face , and at the other there 's a sharp angled drop of around 600 metres down to a valley and village below . @@137861767 <h> US plans to fight flesh-eating screwworm outbreak with flies and dogs <p> 22 hours ago <p> Max Matza <p> Reuters <p> US agriculture and health officials have outlined a plan to combat a flesh-eating parasite that has been detected in the US for the first time since 1966 . <p> The plan to prevent a US outbreak of the New World Screwworm focuses on deploying hundreds of millions of genetically-altered sterile flies . Experts , though , say the supply of sterile flies is too low to immediately impact and halt the growing screwworm population . <p> Other measures include establishing a containment zone around the site of the first US infection along the southern US border , and using sniffer dogs to detect the insects . <p> The threat to humans is low , but cattle ranchers fear an outbreak could have a large impact on beef markets . <p> Screwworms are parasitic flies whose females lay eggs in open wounds and mucous membranes of living warm-blooded animals and people . When the eggs hatch , hundreds of larvae burrow through living flesh with sharp mouths , eventually @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , US officials announced that the first case in 60 years was detected in a three-week-old calf , with the larvae found in its umbilical area . The discovery was made in the town of La Pryor , Texas , about 30 miles ( 48km ) from the Mexico border . <p> Officials have set up a 20km-wide " control zone " , and are " implementing quarantines , movement controls , and surveillance in this area , " according to the US Department of Agriculture ( USDA ) . <p> Screwworm larvae grow into flies which can travel short distances . The primary way that they have travelled long distances is by being brought by humans . There have been a handful of US cases since 1966 , when travellers brought the pest back , but no larger outbreaks . <p> Officials in the US and in Latin America have been combating the problem of screwworms for much of the past six decades , with limited success . <p> Getty Images <p> Screwworms grow after hatching from flesh , and can grow to be twice as large as the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is by releasing hundreds of millions of sterile screwworm flies , as the females only mate once in their lifetime , and any eggs they lay will be unfertilised and will not hatch . <p> This method , known as the Sterile Insect Technique , has been in use for many years to control a variety of insect populations , including fruit flies and mosquitos . It works by hatching flies in an enclosed space , and then exposing them to radiation to make them sterile before releasing them into the wild . <p> However , officials say that they will need to breed up to 600 million sterile screwworms flies each week in order to fight back the outbreak . <p> Currently , facilities in the US and Mexico are only capable of producing about 100 million sterile flies per week . <p> US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins told reporters on Thursday that since the discovery of the infected calf , officials have released four million sterile flies by ground , in addition to another four million that they have been releasing by plane on a weekly basis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ believe that this incursion will result in any sort of establishment of the pests , " said Rollins . <p> But critics , including cattle farmers in Texas , are worried it 's not enough and some have accused the Trump administration of not taking the problem seriously . <p> The last outbreak that came close to threatening American cattle was in the 1970s , but at that time no screwworms were ever found inside the US . <p> The use of sterile flies pushed the screwworms south below the Darien Gap , Panama 's heavily-forested border region with Colombia . @@137862755 <h> Book review : Promise the Earth : A safe climate in good faith by Julian Allwood and Andrew Davison <p> by <p> 05 June 2026 <p> James Currall reviews a discussion of climate change and ethics <p> WHETHER you dismiss much of the debate about the " climate crisis " as scaremongering or as something that worries you , but you feel that you ca n't do anything about it , then perhaps you have something to learn from this unique collaboration between an engineer and a theologian . It is a book that combines practical scientific/engineering explanation with a discussion of traditional and Christian virtues . <p> Between the introduction and the conclusion , there are 14 chapters , which alternate between practical matters : urgency , innovation , restraint , cost , action , leadership , and decisions , and the four cardinal virtues : courage , prudence , temperance , and justice , plus the three Christian virtues : faith , hope , and love . There are also fifty pages of supporting appendices and notes , primarily supporting the odd-numbered chapters on practical matters . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ matters , and the remainder concerns the virtues . <p> The even-numbered virtue chapters provide plenty to reflect on in terms of how to live a " good " life . They are relatively short and written in a very gentle but persuasive style , and I enjoyed engaging with them . I find myself , however , a little conflicted about the more practical chapters and accompanying appendices . <p> These practical chapters lay out very clearly the challenge of reducing greenhouse gases to halt the progress of global warming . Their premise is simple : it is no use waiting for new technologies to come along and save the day -- the often unstated assumption of politicians and other leaders in industry and elsewhere . Such " convenient solutions " can neither be developed nor deployed in the relatively short period between now and when global warming reaches the point of " no return " in about 2050 . If humanity are to avoid this , we collectively have to stop kicking the can down the road and start taking both individual and collective action now -- and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Failure to achieve this goal means that increasing areas of the world will become unsuitable for food production , and their populations will migrate to areas where food production is still possible . This will be at a scale that will give political leaders nightmares beyond their wildest imaginings and ultimately lead to global wars between starving migrants and countries trying to hold them back . <p> To be clear , I am largely in agreement with that premise and predictions , which are well supported by the appendices with their tables and graphs . The " way forward " proposed is that humanity , especially in the developed world , has willingly ( with restraint ) or unwillingly ( with constraint ) to eliminate the biggest contributors to greenhouse gasses : <p> the use of fossil fuels in boilers for heating and cars , trucks , ships , and planes ; <p> the production and use of cement ; <p> the rearing and consumption and use of ruminant animals ( cattle and sheep , including dairy products ) ; and <p> the cultivation and use of conventionally grown @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ purposes . <p> Now , for me , if one dismisses the idea of technology coming to the rescue , it is a big leap to imagine that wholesale behavioural change is going to happen , especially against a background of increasingly bellicose and extravagant political rhetoric . Yes , an increasing proportion of the population might embrace the cardinal and Christian virtues as a result of recognising their moral responsibilities to the rest of humanity and the planet , or becoming ever more worried by what is happening to the global climate ; but will that scratch the surface of the problem ? Can you imagine politicians setting out their stall on that basis and hoping to remain in power ? <p> I like the premise of this book : it is a refreshing change of approach , and I would recommend it as an excellent bridge between faith and the science ( many of the ideas expressed therein mirror my own in a series of lectures in 2023 ) . Its leap of faith , however , matches a cartoon that I saw years ago , in which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a chalkboard covered in equations which end with " . . . and then a miracle occurs . " <p> The Revd Dr James Currall is an environmental scientist and retired priest of congregations in Sutherland and Easter Ross , in the Highlands of Scotland . <p> Promise the Earth : A safe climate in good faithJulian Allwood and Andrew DavisonCambridge University Press ? 15.99 ( 978-1-009-56399-4 ) Church Times Bookshop ? 14.39 <h> Welcome to the Church Times <p> To explore the Church Times website fully , please sign in or subscribe . <p> New to us ? Then , if you want to push your performance further or you enjoy a particular type of exercise , you can do more when life allows . <p> For me , during a recent week-long road trip around Scotland with friends , this meant having some form of protein and vegetables with each meal , doing a quick bit of movement each morning ( whether that was a stretching session or a short bodyweight workout ) , sleeping in when tired and walking a lot -- easy to do in the Highlands . <p> But what I did n't do was turn down a trip to a bakery or a late-night chance to spot orcas off John O'Groats just because these clashed with optimal health advice . <p> What optimisation advocates often overlook are the science-backed longevity perks of socialising , purpose and friendship . Sometimes these stand at odds with their definition of " optimal " living , but for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trade-off is often worth making . There is health to be found in happiness . <p> To support this point , I 'm going to turn to my time as a reporter for a regional newspaper . Colleagues and I would write stories about local people celebrating their 100th birthdays , and each time we would ask them the secret to reaching the milestone . Not one person named a supplement or specific protocol . <p> " Brandy and biscuits " came up more than once . Not consumed by the bucketload , but as a treat that brought people joy every now and then -- balance in action . Staying active also earned recurring mentions , as did spending time with friends and loved ones . <p> Genetics play a considerable role in longevity , but from my experience , happiness and/or purpose are also fairly common denominators among those who reach a century . <p> On the flip side , some of the worst nights of sleep I 've endured came when I was worrying about getting enough sleep . Obsessing over my stress levels has , in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what conclusions can we draw from this ? Health and happiness make for excellent bedfellows , and one should not come at the expense of the other . <p> Something is better than nothing on the fitness front , whether that 's a short bout of morning movement or a few extra vegetables with your meals . But you only need to do enough to keep you healthy and happy , and fixating on this should not detract from your ability to live a life you love . <h> Get the Well Enough newsletter <p> Get the Well Enough newsletter with Harry Bullmore ( The Independent ) <p> To receive Well Enough with Harry Bullmore , simply enter your email address in the box at the top of this page .

" There have been many studies looking at variations in AMOC strength over time , and most of these reveal a weakening , " says McGuire . One study suggests that the AMOC has weakened by 15 per cent since the mid-20th century . A 2024 study has found that it has weakened further during every decade since 1950 . <p> The AMOC is failing because of the " cold blob , " which has formed thanks to the rapid melting of Greenland 's ice sheets . And , by and large , GB News viewers have no complaints . <p> Most of our 20 reviewers had never watched GB @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not by the political views that dominate the station 's output , but by the way the channel is driving a coach and horses through the laws that were put in place to define broadcasting in the UK . <p> The UK news ecosystem is both special and unique . Newspapers have , for 200 years , often been wildly opinionated in their approach to journalism . But parliament decided that broadcasting would be different : in return for a licence , there 's an obligation to be accurate and impartial . Broadcasters are required to offer appropriate challenge and context , and are supposed to promote a range of viewpoints . <p> GB News routinely -- you might almost say systematically -- disregards these requirements . Asked to score the programmes on a scale of 0-5 ( 0 being not at all compliant with Ofcom 's Broadcasting Code and 5 being wholly compliant ) , the overall score from our reviewers was just 1.5 . Each reviewer came up with detailed reasoning . <p> Ofcom 's log of complaints , by contrast , shows a tiny trickle of concern @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ triggered no complaints , two sparked two complaints , while a kid-glove interview with Donald Trump led to 32 . @@137972137 <p> This is an impossibly lovely book , written by a Benedictine monk and beekeeper . We learn early on that these two callings are symbiotic . Many spiritual writers have written on the harmony of the hive and the moral lessons to be drawn from bees . Monks and bees live in community . And from everything Gabriel Wilson writes -- in delicious , sensuous prose -- it is clear that working with bees entails the active and contemplative virtues . <p> Much of the time , this beekeeper simply listens to his bees , watches and waits . When he intervenes it is with care for the season and the condition of the hive . Indeed one of his most eloquent accounts is of a beekeeper -- is it he ? -- who does next to nothing , who does not use a fumigator nor curb the parasites on the creatures but simply leaves well alone , to the bemusement of his fellow apiarists . The latest projection , released on June 9 , 2026 , is that the Social Security trust fund will be depleted by 2032 , at which point incoming revenue can pay only about 78% of scheduled benefits . <p> For the 1 in 5 Americans who receive Social Security , that means a potential across-the-board benefit cut of roughly 22% unless Congress acts . <p> What makes this year 's warning especially troubling is that the deterioration is n't driven by a temporary downturn but by deeper demographic and policy changes : Fewer expected births , lower immigration , slower growth in the workforce and reduced future revenue from the taxation of Social Security benefits . <p> There are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ number of retirees ( Getty Images ) <p> The fundamental challenge , though , has been obvious for years . There are too few current and future workers to support the growing number of retirees . And now , there are fresh headwinds that make the math even more daunting . Record debt levels and elevated interest rates are reducing the fiscal resources available for lawmakers to implement solutions , while declining immigration and birth rates mean that the supply of current and future workers is even smaller than previously projected . <p> These pressures do n't mean Social Security will disappear . It will always exist as long as workers and employers pay into the program . Public debt is projected to rise to 120% of GDP by 2036 , leaving less and less fiscal room to patch Social Security . <p> Servicing that debt is also becoming more expensive . Although the Federal Reserve trimmed interest rates in 2024 and 2025 , the cost of borrowing remains elevated as concerns over inflation grow , exacerbated by oil price spikes and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a while , and some investors are betting it may even raise them later this year . <p> The demographic picture is also unforgiving . The result is fewer future workers paying payroll taxes , even as the number of retirees grows . <p> A final factor is immigration . <p> While other aging countries have turned to immigration to shore up public finances and revitalize their labor force , the U.S. has taken the opposite approach . @@138066670 <h> The sites fighting to be removed from the Unesco World Heritage List <p> It recognises places of " outstanding universal value " and can catapult lesser-known sites to global fame . So why are some places pleading to be removed from the list ? <p> Set in the mountains of central Slovakia , the tiny village of Vlkol ? nec is a picture-perfect medieval hamlet with more houses than people . Its roughly 20 full-time residents live in 45 fairytale-like cottages painted in bright colours clustered around an 18th-Century bell tower . <p> Because of Vlkol ? nec 's distinctive architecture , this remarkably intact settlement was added by the United Nations as a World Heritage site in 1993 . Since then , more than 100,000 visitors have descended on the community every year . Recently , some locals have argued that the designation and associated tourism has created more issues than they 're worth and want to have the village delisted . <p> Roughly 7,000km away in Tanzania , the Maasai International Solidarity Alliance has also called for removing the wildlife-rich Ngorongoro Conservation Area from the World Heritage @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some of Africa 's most iconic safari experiences , but locals argue that conservation policies tied to its internationally protected status have led to residents being displaced from ancestral grazing lands . <p> These disputes are highlighting a growing debate about what happens when the interests of local communities collide with efforts to preserve places deemed important to humanity . <p> Getty Images <p> Unesco 's 1,248 World Heritage sites include World Wonders as well as lesser-known landmarks ( Credit : Getty Images ) <h> Unesco 's power <p> The ever-expanding World Heritage List is overseen by Unesco , an international United Nations committee that identifies and protects places it deems to have " outstanding cultural or natural importance to humanity " . Since it inscribed its first 12 sites in 1978 , its list has grown to 1,248 sites across 170 countries . These range from famous landmarks such as Machu Picchu and the Great Wall of China to lesser-known places such as Romania 's Wooden Churches of Maramure ? and the ancient Moroccan oasis settlements of Ait-Ben-Haddou . <p> The World Heritage List emerged from a post-World War @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by conflict , industrialisation and modern development . <p> Because Unesco designation can unlock international conservation funding , it is one of the world 's most influential tools for heritage protection . Supporters point to examples such as the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System , which was removed from Unesco 's " In Danger " list in 2018 after stronger environmental protections were introduced ; and Angkor Wat , where decades of restoration and conservation work helped save a site badly damaged by war and looting . <p> " The credo of Unesco is about shared heritage , conserving it , celebrating it and recognising it as an accomplishment of humankind , " says John H Stubbs , a preservation scholar and former vice president at the World Monuments Fund . <p> But since the World Heritage List 's early days , the rise of social media has increasingly made Unesco status something that may help to preserve a site while simultaneously changing the communities who live nearby through tourism . <p> Alamy <p> Venice is now one of Europe 's most overtouristed places ( Credit : Alamy ) <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ overtourism , compares the Unesco designation to star ratings in guidebooks that point tourists to " must-see " places . He also notes that more visitors is one of the most predictable results of being added to the list . <p> " I think the consensus among the leading experts in the world is that there is a whole range of possible things that can result from getting a Unesco listing , but one that will definitely happen is increased visitation . " <h> Preservation and ' museumification ' <p> Historically , Unesco preservation efforts were primarily focused on protecting physical structures : monuments , archaeological sites and architecturally significant buildings . But many modern heritage destinations now overlap with communities where residents still live and work . <p> Venice , Italy , which became a Unesco World Heritage site in 1987 , has seen such increased tourism that the city has become one of Europe 's most overtouristed places -- and more residents are leaving as a result . In Lijiang , China , a city known for its Old Town and Naxi Indigenous culture , tourism increased after @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ areas filled with guesthouses and souvenir shops that some researchers and residents say have diluted local life . In Marrakesh , Morocco , more tourism and foreign investment in the Unesco-listed medina have sparked debates about rising property prices and gentrification . <p> Getty Images <p> Unesco sites can modernise , but they have to preserve the site 's " outstanding universal value " ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Researchers sometimes describe the process as " museumification " : the gradual transformation of living communities into places increasingly oriented around visitors rather than residents . While many historic communities were already grappling with housing shortages and economic change long before Unesco recognition , in some cases -- as with Venice -- tourism merely accelerates existing trends . <p> The debate grows even more tangled as ideas about authenticity and preservation evolve . <p> " This is one of the big debates in heritage conservation , " Richards says . " Authenticity is a very dangerous word because it can be interpreted in all sorts of different ways . " He explains that what one group sees as authentic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Unesco sites are not prohibited from modernising , but developments are expected to preserve what the organisation calls a site 's " outstanding universal value " -- the defining qualities that earned it designation in the first place . In practice , that can create tensions between preservation and contemporary needs , particularly in communities that still require updated housing and infrastructure . <p> Richards also says that social media has greatly accelerated the pace at which tourism pressure builds . Before platforms like TikTok and Instagram , travellers mostly used guidebooks or official tourism information . " Now , increasingly , you 're following other tourists , " he says . <p> Getty Images <p> The Ngorongoro is home to some of Africa 's most iconic safari experiences ( Credit : Getty Images ) <h> Unesco 's new tourism approach <p> Representatives say Unesco is becoming more aware that World Heritage Sites are prone to overtourism . <p> " We certainly recognise that tourism has changed dramatically over the last 10 to 15 years , " says Peter DeBrine , a Unesco sustainable tourism specialist . He adds that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for tourism growth and find ways to reduce crowding and pressure on sensitive areas . <p> " We 're not trying to discourage tourism at all , but just help that tourism to support conservation and the heritage , " he says . " World Heritage Sites are there for everybody . They 're for all humanity . We do want people to visit them , to experience them . " <p> The shift reflects a broader evolution in Unesco 's approach . In Unesco 's early World Heritage guidance documents , tourism was mentioned only briefly and largely in the context of its potential impacts on conservation , according to DeBrine . <p> Getty Images <p> Locals have argued that Ngorongoro 's Unesco inclusion has led to residents being displaced from ancestral grazing lands ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Today , Unesco increasingly views tourism as both a challenge and an opportunity -- one that can be a force for conservation and local economies when carefully managed . <p> But the concerns emerging from Vlkol ? nec and Ngorongoro fall outside the World Heritage system 's scope @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a site 's conservation , its role is less clear when the grievance comes not from damage to the site itself , but from the people living within it . <p> When asked if Unesco can step in when local residents feel that tourism or preservation policies are hurting their lives , DeBrine said , " We do n't really have a mechanism for that . " <p> Despite the calls from Vlkol ? nec and Ngorongoro 's Maasai advocacy group to reconsider their World Heritage status , neither site is expected to be discussed by the World Heritage Committee at its upcoming session . <p> Unesco can currently evaluate whether a landscape , monument or ecosystem is being adequately protected . It can list sites as " in danger " due to factors like armed conflict , climate change and uncontrolled development . It can also demand conservation measures , or -- in rare cases -- remove a designation altogether . But it ca n't list sites as " in danger " due to the tourism it helped create . <p> Getty Images <p> The Arabian Oryx Sanctuary was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( Credit : Getty Images ) <h> How to lose World Heritage status <p> To date , Unesco has only removed three sites from the World Heritage List , and in each case , the issue centered on conservation . In 2007 , the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary became the first site to be removed after Oman sharply reduced the protected area amid plans for oil exploration . In 2009 , Dresden Elbe Valley lost its status following the construction of a bridge , which Unesco argued fundamentally altered the landscape . And in 2021 , Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City was delisted after disputes over waterfront redevelopment . <p> Interestingly , losing Unesco recognition has not always resulted in dramatic tourism declines . Liverpool continued attracting visitors tied to its music , sports and cultural identity after losing World Heritage status , while Dresden also remained a major tourism destination after its delisting . <p> Despite residents in Vlkol ? nec and Ngorongoro advocating to be removed from the list , Stubbs argues that this is unlikely to result in any meaningful change . <p> " I think it 's great @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the problems of overtourism , " he says . " But in terms of the actual solution that will benefit the locals , as well as the monument , the answer is going to come from smart conservation planning that takes into account everything from economics to location to local people . " <p> More than half a century after Unesco set out to preserve its first sites , the debates suggest that saving a place is not the same as saving a community -- and that the latter may prove far more difficult .

The genetic analysis shows that the Cheviot population has not crossbred with other goats at all . <p> ? <p> Researchers also found that the population has low genetic diversity and is highly inbred @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ culling practices . Locally adapted breeds in small , isolated populations like the Cheviot goats are particularly prone to genomic erosion ( the loss of genetic diversity ) and so future work should consider incorporating genetic information to enable effective decision-making in future breed conservation strategies . @@138119641 <p> The relentless squeeze on our finances will continue next month when a typical energy bill will soar by ? 221 to a whopping ? 1,862 a year . <p> This most unwelcome rise will push millions of homes even closer to breaking point . Calls for net zero to be delayed or scrapped are never far away , and former prime minister Sir Tony Blair joined those voices a couple of weeks ago . In his foreword to the Tony Blair Institute 's The Climate Paradox : Why We Need to Reset Action on Climate Change , he writes that " any strategy based on either ' phasing out ' fossil fuels in the short term or limiting consumption is a strategy doomed to fail " . <p> But the truth is that , however bad the bill rises are , things would have been even worse if it were n't for the miles of solar panels and wind turbines that have sprung up around the country in recent years . These are providing valuable -- if insufficient -- protection against gas prices sent soaring by the Iran war @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by 28 per cent on 1 July , when energy regulator Ofgem introduces its next three-monthly price cap . <p> That gas prices have only dragged up electricity prices a little bit is a significant and welcome development . As recently as the six months from April to the end of September 2022 , things were very different . Gas and electricity prices were much more closely linked , and when the Ukraine war broke out , it sent gas prices up by 100 per cent ; electricity went up by nearly as much , a whopping 83 per cent . <p> So what has changed ? The main reason is that , after a building spree , solar and wind are producing a lot more of the electricity we use today than they were four years ago -- meaning that gas is being used much less . <p> Because it typically costs less than half as much to produce electricity from wind and solar as it does from gas , the surge in renewable energy means that the prevailing market price of electricity at any given time ( which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it is generated ) is being set far less often by costly gas and far more often by cheaper wind and solar . <p> This means that household energy bills are now partially protected from the impact of soaring gas prices -- although with 84 per cent of homes still using gas central heating , the protective effect is far less than it could be if households could afford to switch to heat pumps , which run on electricity . <p> Electricity bills are further protected by agreements between governments and energy suppliers , known as Contracts for Difference , which set a fixed price for the renewable electricity . These are more favourable when the gas price spikes , helping to stop electricity bills rising -- and the Government is pushing more generators to sign up to these fixed-price contracts by forcing them to pay higher taxes if they do n't . <p> But even though the effects of high gas prices on electricity prices are being curbed , electricity is still far more expensive than it should be . <p> It may sound surprising , but electricity prices @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gas . This is actually far better than it was in 2021 and 2022 , when electricity was nearly six times as expensive as gas . <p> But this price disparity is still a significant barrier for many people wanting to switch to electric vehicles or electric heat pumps from petrol cars and gas central heating , even though the electric alternatives are generally much more efficient to run . <p> Part of the disparity ca n't really be helped . Electricity has higher transmission and distribution costs -- high-voltage power lines , transformers and substations are more expensive to build and maintain than gas pipelines , which can transport large quantities of gas over long distances relatively cheaply . <p> But there is another key factor that can be addressed . Levies to support green measures and help low-income families with energy bills have mostly been put onto electricity bills , with gas bills far less affected . <p> The Government took steps to improve the situation with its last budget in November , when it knocked ? 150 worth of levies off the average annual electricity bill and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the average electricity bill still has around ? 120 of levies on it , which need to come off . If they were also put into general taxation , this would bring the cost of electricity down to 3.2 times that of gas , according to the UK Electricity Bills Taskforce . And if they were put onto gas bills instead , which is possible but not likely , that would reduce the ratio further . <p> Given that heat pumps are typically three to five times more efficient than gas boilers at producing heat , these reductions could end up pushing thousands of households into making the switch -- especially with most homes eligible for a ? 7,500 heat pump grant . <p> At the same time , continuing the wind and solar building spree will bring electricity prices down further by replacing more gas generation . With a record number of renewable projects approved in 2025 , which will contribute 96 per cent more energy capacity than projects approved in 2024 , the next 10 years look promising if bottlenecks in the grid can be fixed . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ generation , the less volatile your bills will be . <p> And this is why Blair 's call for the UK to ditch its target of achieving net- zero by 2050 and to ramp up North Sea oil and gas production was a bad idea . The more renewable energy we can generate in the UK , the cheaper our bills and the greater our energy security , as we are further freed from the rollercoaster of gas prices .

At the end of the first act , Katie , a young mother relocated from London to Newcastle due to a lack of social housing , goes into a food bank for the first time . Daniel dies the night before his hearing , but even this does not extinguish the spirit of hope . The final scene focuses on Katie at Dan 's funeral . Although it is a ' pauper 's service ' , he is sent off by the people who love him . The government , the play suggests , might not be on the side of working people , but the community is -- and it is from our community that we draw hope . <p> I , Daniel Blake has had a palpable political impact . The moments of joy in the play come from a perpetual hope . @@138155504 <h> The US Government Is Letting a Key Data Center Regulation Expire <p> The federal government is planning to let a rule regulating federal data center operations sunset in September with no replacement . <p> Photograph : Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images <p> The US government is quietly planning to allow a rule outlining the standards for federal data center usage and operations , known as the Federal Data Center Enhancement Act ( FDCEA ) , to expire , according to sources who spoke to WIRED . This , current and former workers at OMB and the General Services Administration ( GSA ) say , signals that the Trump administration is set to take an even more hands-off approach to data center oversight and regulation . <p> A replacement for the requirements laid out in FDCEA would , in other administrations , have been in the works for months ahead of its expiration . This year 's event will see the launch of the first-ever sustainable agriculture tent , which is set to showcase a variety of innovations from farms across the country . <p> Agriculture is the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Scotland , with the sector 's contribution amounting to approximately 19% of the national total . <p> In order to achieve Scottish Government targets of halting biodiversity loss by 2030 and reaching Net Zero emissions by 2045 , a greater focus on agricultural emissions , pollution , and land usage is required . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to support a just transition for farmers , and organisations such as the James Hutton Institute are already pioneering projects that reduce the impacts of agriculture while remaining profitable . <h> Animal agriculture and methane reduction <p> Animal agriculture accounts for approximately 60% of all agricultural emissions , with the beef industry being the primary offender . The demand for meat and dairy products is rising globally , though climate scientists warn that cutting livestock emissions by at least 61% by 2035 is essential for aligning with the goals of the Paris Agreement and keeping global heating below 1.5 ? C. <p> Cows in methane-removal shed ( Image : Green Shed/SRUC ) <p> Scotland 's Rural College ( SRUC ) is pioneering research into methods of reducing emissions in the beef and dairy industries , focusing on areas such as selective breeding for low-methane animals and developing methane-suppressing feed products . <p> SRUC is also trialling a circular farming system designed to trap emissions generated by cattle and repurpose their waste as fuel . GreenShed 's methane-capture system is powered by a mixture of the gas it collects and biogas @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ terms of energy requirements . <p> The solid by-product of biogas production is also used as a low-carbon fertiliser for indoor crops such as lettuce and pak choi . <p> It is estimated that this system could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 237 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per farm annually , and in future , researchers on the project intend to trial methane-eating microbes to further reduce emissions . <p> Yet the environmental issues caused by the meat and dairy industries extend far beyond emissions . Across the globe , approximately 80% of farmland is used for rearing and feeding livestock , while only accounting for 18% of the calories we consume . <p> While it may be common knowledge that the demand for pasture is driving deforestation in the Amazon rainforest , we are also seeing the environmental impacts of intensive animal agriculture in Scotland , with overgrazing contributing to soil erosion , habitat destruction , and biodiversity loss . <h> Breeding Net Zero Crops <p> The overuse of fertiliser in agriculture is responsible for the majority of nitrous oxide gas released into the atmosphere . Plants @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on fields and the remainder is either converted into this potent greenhouse gas by bacteria in the soil or washed into waterways during heavy rainfall . <p> Through selective breeding , the James Hutton Institute is working to develop crops that use nitrogen more efficiently , in an effort to reduce emissions and curb agricultural pollution . <p> This is one several features being targeted as part of the project , and plants are also being bred for their ability to remove carbon from the atmosphere and store it . <p> According to the International Barley Hub , most plants capture only a fraction of the carbon they are theoretically capable of absorbing , and by producing a plant with optimal photosynthetic efficiency , carbon fixation capacity could be increased from a maximum of 7% to as high as 40% . <p> As climate change poses an increased risk of droughts and flooding , the importance of cultivating crops that can better withstand extreme weather conditions is becoming more apparent . An example of this is plants with deeper root networks , which enable them to reach water sources during @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the International Barley Hub , explains : " We can develop varieties that can cope with a range of stressors , but the Holy Grail is developing a genotype that can cope with all of these , because we 're seeing more variation in the weather year on year . " <p> However , George suggests that a more realistic outcome would be a " patchwork " of varieties that meet the needs of different areas and have the added benefit of safeguarding against disease and strengthening food security by ensuring greater genetic diversity . <h> Rewilding to reduce fertiliser run-off <p> Fertiliser run-off is a major cause of pollution in Scotland 's waterways , with approximately 9,000 tonnes of soil being lost annually . During periods of rainfall , excess nitrogen and phosphorus are washed into rivers and lochs , causing algal blooms that ultimately deplete them of oxygen and suffocate other aquatic life . <p> The strips of land that border rivers , known as riparian zones , can be modified in simple ways that have a dramatic impact on the health of ecosystems . Introducing native @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ binding the soil , which helps to reduce fertiliser run-off and traps pollutants . <p> The Riverwoods partnership currently has 162 projects running across Scotland , with 968,400 trees having been planted so far . Restoring riparian woodlands provides habitats for birds and mammals , but also lowers water temperatures by providing shade , creating better conditions for species such as the Atlantic salmon , which are sensitive to higher temperatures . <p> The James Hutton Institute has also been conducting research into managing riparian zones , particularly through the approach that has been dubbed " magic margins " . <p> These consist of a series of artificial soil ridges that run parallel to a river and function by slowing the flow of water on sloped land , trapping nutrients and agrochemicals , which are then absorbed by perennial vegetation . This simple and cost-effective method of reducing runoff and soil erosion and can be created using conventional farming equipment such as a potato plough . <p> Research is increasingly turning to digital technology as a means of assisting climate change adaptation . One example of this is OurSmartFarm , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and data modelling to help farmers anticipate weather conditions , identify issues with crop and soil health , and make informed land management decisions . <p> Dr Mike Rivington , a land use system modeller at OurSmartFarm , said : " One of the tools that we have allows farmers to create their own management scenarios of how much fertiliser they might put on . So , rather than experiment in the field , they can experiment on a laptop to inform their decisions . The whole motivation is to help farmers make better decisions for their businesses but also minimise the environmental impact . " <p> For these tools to be effective , collaboration between scientists and farmers is required , with farmers sharing data from sources such as onsite weather stations and soil analyses to enable OurSmartFarm to better calibrate models and provide tailored recommendations . <p> Though this technology is still undergoing development , researchers hope that , in the coming years , more advanced simulation models will enable farmers to project how crop yields could change according to unstable weather patterns caused by climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ driver of biodiversity loss in Scotland and the use of pesticides plays a significant role in this . Chemical run-off permeates habitats , both on land and in freshwater , and the toxicological effect on non-target species , including pollinators , is a major concern . <p> In response to this , the James Hutton Institute is conducting research into integrated pest management ( IPM ) : a combination of strategies intended to limit the need for chemical interventions . These include developing resistant varieties of crops , improving pest identification , and promoting conservation biological control . <p> Researchers say that restoring habitats such as hedgerows and wildflower margins could help to reduce pest populations by increasing biodiversity on farmland and encouraging predators , such as birds and insect species that feed on crop pests . <p> Rising temperatures as a result of climate change have the potential to bring non-native pests and weeds , such as black grass , northward into Scotland , making more robust pest management plans necessary for the coming years . <p> While pesticides may be necessary in some circumstances , researchers advocate applying @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Dr Graham Begg , the head of the James Hutton Institute 's agroecology group , warns : " we should not rely on a silver bullet when that silver bullet can have lots of collateral damage associated with it . " <p> However , farmers often consider moving away from conventional to be a financial and operational risk . Begg perceives this to be symptomatic of a broader social issue and advocates for greater support in the transition to a more sustainable agricultural system . " There was a push to increase productivity post Second World War , which established a way of doing things that has not been optimal for long-term sustainability . <p> " Farmers feel that they are taking the blame for that , when they were only responding to the policy drivers at the time . The biggest difficulty has been that farmers have not been included in discussions on changing policy needs . @@138174497 <h> ' On shore , their weight becomes lethal ' : Why it 's so hard to help a stranded whale <p> 13 hours ago <p> Ally Hirschlag <p> Getty Images <p> The sad fate of a stranded humpback in Germany raises bigger questions about distressed whales -- and how to help them . <p> On 14 May 2026 , the carcass of a 12-metre-long humpback whale washed up in the shallows of Anholt , a small island near Denmark . It rocked back and forth in the waves , occasionally pecked at by seagulls . During that time , and through several failed rescue attempts , he amassed millions of avid fans worldwide , rallying for his life . <p> Many details of Timmy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an important , bigger question : how do you best help a stranded whale ? With strandings rising in some parts of the world , it 's an increasingly important question . <h> A dramatic rise <p> Marine mammal strandings are increasing dramatically in areas where coastal water temperatures are rising due to climate change , like the UK . Scotland saw an 800% increase in baleen whale strandings over the 30 years from 1992 to 2022 , according to a report by the Scottish Marine Animal Stranding Scheme ( SMASS ) . While there 's no singular reason for the spike , the researchers posited that warming waters pushing prey north played a part , along with more plastic and noise pollution from ship traffic . <p> Whale strandings can happen for many reasons , but often it 's because the animal is sick or injured , experts say . <p> " The two most common anthropogenic sources of trauma that lead to stranding are collisions with vessels and entanglement in fishing gear , " says Andrew Read , professor of marine biology and director of Duke University Marine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strand , either alive or dead , if they are sick . Diseased individuals typically exhibit signs of prolonged illness , such as poor body condition . " <p> Stranding response teams from US government agency National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration ( NOAA ) Fisheries see evidence of this in examinations and necropsies . Sometimes it 's a combination of factors , including malnutrition , biotoxins , and young calves being separated from their mothers , says Rachel Hager , lead for public affairs at NOAA Fisheries . <p> Algal blooms , for example , can release biotoxins that sicken whales , causing them to strand . These blooms can also inadvertently lead to strandings by creating " dead zones " , pockets of extremely low dissolved oxygen that form when large algal blooms die and break down on the ocean floor . Dead zones can kill off a whale 's food supply , forcing them to wander closer to shore , where they get stranded . ( Read more about the hidden dead zones spreading across the Baltic Sea floor ) . <p> Weather changes can also disorient whales @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a mass false killer whale strandings off Tasmania in 2025 . " Some whales may have stranded due to making a navigational error , or for social reasons -- if one member of a pod strands , we can see the other pod members strand with them as they try to remain together , " says Natalie Arrow , a marine veterinarian and director of the Marine Mammal Vet and volunteer with the British Divers Marine Life Rescue ( BDMLR ) , which deals with whale strandings . <p> It was the worst mass stranding Tasmania had seen in 50 years , and sadly , due to the powerful surf , none of the animals could be saved . <p> The sheer size of whales is one reason why it 's so hard to help them without further distressing them . Smaller cetaceans like dolphins and porpoises may be carried back to the water for refloating , experts say , but the process is much more difficult for whales . " They typically can not be moved in a way that is both safe for humans and does n't cause @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Arrow . " A humpback whale can reach up to 40,000kg 88,000lb , and blue whales 140,000kg ( 309,000lb ) . " That 's the equivalent of 30 African elephants . A stranded whale with a 7.5-metre-long tail could unintentionally kill you if you were standing near it as it swooshed back and forth . <p> Even when a whale that strands was otherwise healthy , its body can rapidly deteriorate . " Cetaceans are not designed to be on land , and their bodies are impacted by what we call ' stranding-related pathologies ' , " says Arrow . These can include dehydration , injuries from scraping against land , dried-out skin that begins to peel and split , and even hyperthermia because the whale can no longer regulate its body temperature . <p> These animals live in water where their weight is not a concern . But on shore , their weight becomes lethal -- Andrew Read <p> What 's going on inside a stranded whale 's body is even more severe . <p> Symptoms of shock , such as laboured breathing and blood pooling in the stomach @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can begin to crush its internal organs , says Read . " These animals live in water where their weight is not a concern . But on shore , their weight becomes lethal . " <h> If you find a stranded whale <p> If you come upon a stranded whale or any large marine mammal , the first thing you should do is call your local marine mammal stranding network , experts say . In the US , NOAA Fisheries has them listed by region and state . The UK has a few different organisations you can contact based on your location . <p> When you reach them , they 'll ask where you found the stranded animal and whether you can give them any information about its current state ( if it 's moving , what the skin looks like , and whether there are visible wounds , for example ) . If the animal appears to be alive , they 'll instruct you to stay away from it . <p> " We would not recommend approaching the whale without direct advice to do so from the response team @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bystanders around , experts recommend keeping everyone quiet and calm so as not to stress the whale any more . Hager suggests taking pictures of the animal and the scene from different angles and sharing them with the response team so they can keep track of its status . In some instances , if the stranding team deems it safe , bystanders may help keep the animal cool with water . <p> Getty Images <p> Volunteers help a short-finned pilot whale maintain balance during treatment at an animal conservation centre in China in 2024 ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Under no circumstances should people attempt to push or pull the animal back into the water , Hager cautions . Handling or pushing stranded marine mammals back into the water , even if well-intentioned , can count as harassing a protected species , which is illegal in the US , says Hager . <h> When refloating works <p> Once a response team arrives and assesses the whale , they may attempt to refloat it if it 's deemed healthy enough . According to the experts , that 's rarely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " We can almost never perform a controlled refloat of a whale , as they are too large for us to manually move , even with the use of specialist cetacean rescue pontoons that some organisations possess -- they are for small whales only , " says Arrow . <p> A response team may enlist bystanders ' help with smaller whales and other marine mammals if it 's considered safe and appropriate to refloat them . Every stranding scenario is unique , and only a trained team member should make decisions for the animal 's well-being , says Hager . <h> Euthanising a stranded whale <p> Deciding to euthanise a stranded whale -- meaning , killing it to end its suffering -- is never easy , experts say . " Euthanasia is a last resort used to end the suffering of an animal that is deemed unable to survive , " says Jim Rice , stranding programme manager at the Marine Mammal Institute , Oregon State University . <p> However , even if the vets on site believe that it 's the most compassionate course of action , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ very large amount of the medication is needed to compassionately euthanise a whale , and it may be difficult to administer it . Killing the animal with a firearm is also difficult given its thick skin -- and of course , euthanasia by any means requires special authorisation . In the case of Timmy , German officials said that euthanasia was not a feasible option under the circumstances . <p> Then there 's the matter of the remaining animal carcass . If the whale is euthanised with a chemical agent , its body will need to be disposed of properly , since it can poison nearby scavengers . If it died of natural causes or without dangerous chemical aids , the carcass is often left or buried on the beach where it stranded . <p> Given the lack of other options , large whales are often left to die without intervention as it 's " the most humane and practical response " , says Read . This can take anywhere from several hours to a few days . <p> For onlookers , it may feel cruel to leave an animal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the overwhelming compassion and desire to save such a magnificent creature . <p> " Marine mammals bring out very strong emotions in people , most of whom only want what 's best for the animal , " says Rice . But people may have unrealistic expectations about what is feasible for the animal 's survivability , he adds . <p> By the time rescue operations to relocate Timmy were underway , he was already likely in a severely compromised state of health , and survival chances were extremely low , says Arrow . <p> " It is not always in the best interest of the animal to return it to the water , given underlying health conditions , as well as the toll and stress of stranding alive , " says Hager . <p> For people who want to help cetaceans threatened by strandings , a more effective point of intervention may be before the stranding : for example , through initiatives that prevent bycatch and entanglement and thus reduce the overall number of strandings .
