But so far , there is no clear evidence that is harming the Seine 's ecology . Studies and monitoring generally show that the system 's heat exchanges create only small , regulated temperature changes that stay within environmental limits . <p> Pauline Lavaud , the director of climate transition in the city government , says Fra ? cheur de Paris " offers much higher energy and environmental performance than individual cooling systems " . <p> A map of the operating sites of the underground cooling system operated by Fra ? cheur de Paris . Photograph : Lewis Joly/AP <p> This is backed by experts . " The energy consumption should be much less than if the same cooling were provided by modular systems , " said Charles Simpson , a senior researcher in climate change at University College London @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not the only city doing this . Stockholm uses sea water from the Baltic to reduce electricity usage during heatwaves and Toronto uses a cooling system that pulls water from Lake Ontario . Experts said this could work in a mega-city like London , too , but it can not be copied and pasted . <p> Lavaud said : " Developing a district cooling network requires substantial investment . For the project to be economically viable and commercially attractive , a city must have sufficiently concentrated cooling demand ... where a dense network can be justified . " <p> Cost is one big hurdle . The total value of the 20-year contract for Fra ? cheur de Paris was ? 2.4bn ( ? 2bn ) . " The three-day average nighttime temperatures would not have been possible at any time of year without climate change , and the chance of the three-day maximum daily temperatures like this occurring at any time of the year has increased by over 500 times " since 1976 . <p> By 1976 , the planet had heated by just 0.3 C above preindustrial levels , rising to 0.6 C in 2003 and 1.4 C last year . @@138468641 <p> The record-shattering June heat that 's baked Europe this week would have been " virtually impossible " just a few decades ago , according to a new analysis , which says the human-driven climate crisis is " unequivocally to blame . " <p> The ongoing heat wave is the region 's " most severe ever recorded , " according to the study published Friday by World Weather Attribution , a scientific network which analyzes the role of climate change in driving extreme weather events . <p> Huge parts Europe have been suffocating under a stubborn heat dome parked over the continent , trapping hot air and leading to extreme and dangerous heat and humidity . Heat domes are not unusual , but the temperatures in this one have been . <p> Commuters wait on a Paris Metro platform during hot weather on June 24 , 2026 in Paris , France . <p> Annice Lyn/Getty Images <p> To calculate the role climate change played in these extremes , WWA scientists used real-world and forecast data to analyze the three hottest days and nights of this heat wave across a huge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ during past major heat wave years of 1976 and 2003 , when the Earth was cooler . <p> They found both the daytime highs and nighttime temperatures during this period would have been " virtually impossible " 50 years ago , in 1976 , when some of the previous European heat records were set . <p> The world has warmed by nearly 2 degrees Fahrenheit ( 1.1 degrees Celsius ) over the past 50 years , which has increased the chances of extreme heat immensely , the scientists said . <p> A similar heat wave occurring in June 1976 would have been a startling 6.3 degrees Fahrenheit cooler ( 3.5 degrees Celsius ) , according to the study , which has not been peer-reviewed but used peer-reviewed methods . <p> The scientists looked at nighttime temperatures , too , which have also been record-breaking : France endured its hottest night ever recorded Wednesday into Thursday . Heat at night is particularly dangerous because it allows the body no time to recover . <p> Europe 's sweltering nighttime heat is about 100 times more likely today than it was in 2003 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ killed more than 70,000 people , the report found . <p> The WWA scientists also analyzed the impacts of the heat wave 's high humidity . They looked at 854 cities across 30 heat-affected European countries and found 45% of them have broken or are about to break their all-time records for wet bulb globe temperature . <p> Wet bulb globe temperature accounts for the combined impacts of temperature , humidity , sun and wind , and is a measure of heat stress and the body 's ability to cool itself . The higher it gets , the harder it is for the body to rely on its cooling mechanisms , especially sweating , increasing the chances of heat exhaustion or even heat stroke , which can be fatal . <p> Europe 's heat has quickly turned deadly . Although the true extent of deaths wo n't be known for some time , countries have already reported hundreds of heat-related fatalities . <p> In Spain , more than 200 people have died due to the heat wave over just four days , according to data estimates from the country 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ people have drowned in France seeking relief from the heat over the last week . <p> The heat wave also forced thousands of schools to close , disrupted rail services , led to power outages and closed tourist attractions . <p> Europe is the planet 's fastest-warming continent and these kinds of extreme heat waves are only expected to become more severe , frequent and prolonged unless humans rapidly phase out fossil fuels , the scientists said . <p> " It 's really now a question of what kind of future we want for ourselves , and whether we 're willing to do what it takes to secure it . " said Friederike Otto , a professor of climate science at Imperial College London .

@@138473985 <p> Britain 's perfectly mown lawns are putting butterfly populations at risk , according to a new report finding a " loss of habitat " is putting nearly half of UK species at risk . <p> Four fifths of the UK 's butterfly species have declined either in numbers or geographical spread , or both , since the late 70s , the charity Butterfly Conservation found . <p> While a handful of species , such as the Purple Emperor and the Chequered Skipper , appeared to be growing in range thanks in part to climate change , most were suffering due to intensive farming and gardening as well as habitat loss . <p> The data comes from the first update to theState of UK Butterflies report in seven years . These unprecedented high temperatures , which can affect human , animal and plant health , as well as several industries , are due to a weather phenomenon known as an omega block . <h> What is an omega block ? <p> An omega block is reminiscent of the shape of the Greek letter O , with a " bulge of warmer , settled high pressure held between two cooler low-pressure systems , " said Reuters . The high-pressure warmth is essentially " blocked " by the low-pressure systems surrounding it . As a result , " hot , still air gets lodged over the same area , " and " conditions become hot and dry . " The high pressure also " suppresses cloud formation , resulting in clear , sunny skies that allow temperatures to climb . " Omega blocks usually last between three ? and ten days , but can go on for longer . <p> With the current omega block , a " surge of hot , dry air @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ parts of Europe , " said Time . The ingredients that will need to be checked are commonly found in products including chocolate , cooking oils , cosmetics and shampoos , which are readily available in supermarkets for customers to purchase . <p> To take these new regulations forward , the Government plans to use powers found in the Environmental Act as well as strengthening the existing UK Timber Regulations . Under the new proposal , UK businesses who get items sourced from rainforests such as soy , oil , cocoa and rubber will need to check that their supply chains are not contributing to illegal deforestation . <p> The new proposed changes will help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ found in our global rainforests . It will also give British shoppers the assurance that their supermarket staples are not causing illegal harm to the world 's beloved rainforests . <p> Mary Creagh , the Nature Minister , said : " Tackling global deforestation is one of the most effective ways we can address climate change and protect some of the world 's most precious and unique wildlife . <p> " That 's why we are leading by example and scrutinising our own supply chains . Eliminating products linked to illegal deforestation not only helps to protect precious ecosystems but is good for our collective resilience and long-term prosperity . " <p> The Government 's new measures plan to help businesses reduce the risk of their imported ingredients being linked to illegal land clearing and deforestation . Businesses , civil society and international partners will be consulted by the government later this year to be fully informed about the proposed GB deforestation policy . <p> The consultation will include obligatory due diligence requirements for businesses in Great Britain using powers under the Environment Act which target illegal deforestation . Powers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be discussed . <p> The Government 's proposed future plans will then focus on trying to transition to a ' deforestation-free ' standard for businesses to adapt to and follow . If successful , these ambitious plans will then require relevant products to be produced free for any deforestation in the hopes to globally detach supply chains from forest loss and land conversion . <p> Andrew Opie , Director of Food &amp; Sustainability at the BRC , said : " Retailers welcome today 's announcement . We have long called for UK deforestation regulation as an important step in driving forest conservation across retail supply chains in line with business commitments , while supporting alignment with the EU where possible to avoid unnecessary costs and complexity for retailers and their customers . <p> " However , with the EU regulation due to take effect in Northern Ireland at the end of the year , it 's important that the Government takes a pragmatic approach to enforcement to minimise disruption for businesses and consumers . " <p> In Northern Ireland , the EU Regulation on Deforestation-Free Products ( EUDR ) will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Crowden , Director of Advocacy at WWF , said with this in mind , there is ' no excuse ' for any further delays for the rest of the UK following suit . <p> Gavin said : " The UK Government has warned that the collapse of tropical forests in places like the Amazon and Indonesia is a national security risk , not just an environmental one . We rely on these forests for food and climate stability , and they 're home to extraordinary wildlife . <p> " With new rules finally coming into force in Northern Ireland at the end of the year , there 's no excuse for further delay that would leave shoppers in the rest of the UK still unwittingly driving the destruction of the rainforest . <p> Story Saved <p> You can find this story in My Bookmarks.Or by navigating to the user icon in the top right .

June 's full moon , which rises tonight , is a micromoon , and is also known as the Strawberry Moon . The flowers provide abundant nectar and pollen for creatures including bees , butterflies and nocturnal moths . <p> Fresh shoots also draw aphids , which subsequently attract helpful insects such as ladybirds to your garden . <p> Honeysuckle is straightforward to cultivate but requires pruning following summer or winter flowering . Trim away dead , diseased or tangled branches and cut back untidy stems to maintain a healthy appearance . <h> Hardy Geraniums <p> These delightful flowers bring vibrant colour to gardens while acting as powerful attractants for bees and butterflies . Rich in nectar and pollen , they demand minimal upkeep . <p> Trim them substantially after their initial flowering to promote additional blooms later in the season . <h> Ivy <h> Verbena <p> Verbena is particularly attractive to bees and butterflies . @@138581470 <p> KIERA MARSHALL says there is a gulf between the privileged circles in which most politicians move and the lives of working-class youth in left-behind estates -- and as a newly elected Senedd member she 's determined to do something about it <p> HEAT is no longer a future climate risk . It is already here . <p> Across continents , high temperatures are being pushed higher by forces acting at once : human-caused warming , very warm oceans , dry soils , slow-moving high-pressure weather systems and El Nino conditions that have now developed in the tropical Pacific . <p> El Nino is a natural warming of part of the tropical Pacific that can shift weather patterns around the world . It is not the cause of climate change , but when it develops in a climate already warmed by greenhouse gas pollution , it can add another push to global temperatures and regional extremes . <p> The science is clear . Greenhouse gases have raised the baseline , so heatwaves now begin from a warmer starting point . Record ocean heat adds more energy to the climate system @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the sun 's energy goes into evaporating water from soil and plants , and more goes into heating the air . <p> Weather patterns decide where that heat lands . A " heat dome " happens when a high-pressure system settles over a region . Air sinks , clouds are suppressed and temperatures can climb for days . The danger grows when nights remain hot , because bodies , buildings and infrastructure get little chance to cool . <p> El Nino 's effects vary by region and season , so it will not explain every heatwave in 2026 . But it is now being added to long-term warming , and that combination can raise the risk of more extreme heat , drought or heavy rainfall in some regions , including parts of Asia , Australia and the Americas . <p> In Britain , Kew Gardens reached 35.1 ? C in late May , provisionally breaking the national May temperature record for the second day in a row . The previous record , before the 2026 heat , was 32.8 ? C , reached in 1922 and 1944 . <p> Elsewhere @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the hottest spring recorded in France since records began in 1900 . In the United States , March 2026 was the warmest March on record for the contiguous US ( the lower 48 states ) . India 's meteorological service issued an extended heatwave outlook into early July for parts of northern , central and eastern India , while China 's National Climate Centre has forecast above-normal summer temperatures , especially in southern China and Xinjiang in the north-west . In Australia , Tasmania , Victoria and New South Wales have just had one of their 10 warmest autumns on record . <h> Heat kills <p> Heat often kills without leaving obvious damage behind : it pushes bodies past what they can tolerate . <p> High temperatures can cause dehydration , strain the heart , worsen kidney disease and aggravate respiratory illness . Heat can also affect mental health and increase distress . Older people , babies , people with chronic illness , outdoor workers and those living alone are among those at higher risk . <p> Hot nights make heatwaves more dangerous because the body has less chance to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat-related deaths . In an overheated bedroom , care home or hospital ward , strain can continue for hours . <p> The death toll from heat is large , but often underestimated because heat may worsen existing illness rather than appear as the sole cause of death . A 2025 European analysis estimated 62,775 heat-related deaths in Europe in 2024 alone . The Lancet Countdown reports that heat-related deaths among older people have risen sharply , and that hundreds of thousands of people now die globally each year from heat . <p> Heat also puts pressure on the systems people rely on . Hospitals fill faster . Care homes become harder to cool . Rail lines buckle . Roads soften . Rivers warm and water quality declines . Electricity demand rises as people use fans and air-conditioning , while low river flows can affect water quality and supply . A power cut can disrupt cooling , transport , water systems , shops , hospitals and communications . <h> What helps during a heatwave <p> People can reduce risk , especially if they act before they feel ill . <p> Cool @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , take cool showers and put wet cloths on the skin . People who have been told to restrict fluids because of heart failure , kidney disease or another medical condition should follow medical advice about how much to drink . <p> Avoid being outside in the hottest part of the day where possible . Outdoor workers , athletes and people who travel on foot need particular protection . <p> Keep homes cooler before they overheat . Close curtains or blinds during the day , especially on windows facing the sun . Open windows after sunset if it is cooler outside than inside . Sleep in the coolest room available . <p> Check on people at higher risk . Do they have water , shade , medication , a way to get help and somewhere cooler to go if home becomes unsafe ? <p> Take official warnings seriously . Follow heat-health alerts , local weather warnings and public health advice . Have a simple plan for medicines , transport , pets , food , drinking water and somewhere cooler to go if needed . <p> Seek urgent medical help if @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collapses , has very hot skin , has a very high temperature , or does not improve after being moved somewhere cooler and cooled down . <h> Inequality and infrastructure <p> Personal precautions save lives , but they can not make unsafe housing safe , cool a badly ventilated care home or protect outdoor workers without changes to working conditions . <p> Heat risk is shaped by inequality . People without trees , insulation , ventilation , secure work , clean water or affordable energy are less able to avoid exposure , cool their homes or recover after extreme heat . The same pattern applies between countries : communities that have contributed least to climate change are often disproportionately affected , because they have fewer resources for adaptation , healthcare , infrastructure and disaster response . <p> Adapting to heat has to be collective : cooler housing , shaded streets , heat-resilient hospitals , reliable water systems , worker protections , public cooling spaces and early warning systems that reach the people who need them . <p> Heat and drought are increasingly linked emergencies . Heat increases demand for water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they can create failures across health , transport , food , water and energy . Water , health , energy and climate planning need to be connected , because stress in one system can quickly spread to another . <p> The next heatwave will be reported as weather . It should also be understood as a test of housing , healthcare , infrastructure and public protection . A hotter world is already here . The question now is how many heat-related deaths and system failures governments are prepared to accept as normal . <p> Ian Williams is professor of applied environmental science at the University of Southampton .
